title: Six Semesters, Six Different Me’s
webpageTitle: Six Semesters, Six Different Me’s — The Dev Notebook
dek: How my perspective changed every semester of diploma days, and why I’m glad it did.
excerpt: How my perspective changed every semester of college: from pure curiosity to certificates, competitions, an internship lesson, leadership, an intentional friendship, and a no-regrets final semester.
text: Six Semesters, Six Different Me’s How my perspective changed every semester of diploma days, and why I’m glad it did. I was reflecting on the semesters I’ve passed in my diploma college days when I noticed something odd: I never actually decided to change how I see things. It just kept happening, quietly, in the background, like a phone updating overnight. Every semester arrived with its own goals, its own priorities and its own mindset, and looking back, each one was a small upgrade over the one before it. I didn’t notice any of it while it was happening. Only when I laid all six semesters side by side did the pattern show up. So I’m writing it down while it’s still fresh. Think of this as a travel diary, except the place I travelled through was my own head. Pencil sketch of a paper plane flying along a looping dotted trail between two clouds semester 1: no map, just curiosity Fig. 1 — no destination yet, just a lot of sky. SEM 1–2Everything was new In the first two semesters I had no goal and no clarity about what I was supposed to be doing. Everything around me was new: the campus, the people, the rhythm of lectures, the odd freedom of nobody checking your homework every day. I wasn’t chasing anything. I was exploring, taking things in as they came. My perspective was small, and honestly, I think that’s what kept it pure. I went to lectures. I was properly into learning the subjects, not just surviving them. Alongside the syllabus I practised DSA and DP, and I watched YouTube videos on nearly every topic we studied. Not in the panic week before exams, but almost every day. Nobody told me to, and there was no reward waiting. I simply liked the feeling of a concept clicking into place. Then exams would come closer and the mood changed. The library and the quiet corners around campus filled up with a few classmates and me, and I found myself running small lectures for them, mostly on Physics and Chemistry. It was a study group on paper but a classroom without a teacher in practice. Explaining a topic out loud to someone else turned out to be the fastest way to find out whether I actually understood it. I didn’t have a goal yet, but I had curiosity. Looking back, that was enough to start. — note to self SEM 3The certificate I couldn’t explain The first real shift in my perspective began with an embarrassing moment in the 2nd semester, one that took an entire vacation to digest. During the viva for DLS (Development of Life Skills), our professor asked each of us to submit a certificate we had earned. I had nothing. I’d been learning from YouTube for months and had no certificate to show for any of it. So I handed in the only one I had: an appreciation certificate from my society’s internal gathering, given because I had cleared my 10th SSC. Which was, let’s be honest, pretty normal. Not exactly an achievement. Sir looked at it and asked: “What is the significance of this certificate?” “What did you learn from it?” I was blank. Not nervous-blank, but truly empty, because there was no honest answer to give. Sketch of a tilted certificate with a red seal, a speech bubble asking what did you learn from it, and a bubble containing only an ellipsis appreciation what did you learn from it? … my answer, at the time Fig. 2 — the certificate, and the question I couldn’t answer. That silence followed me out of the room. It wasn’t that I hadn’t learned anything. It was that I had nothing I could point to, nothing that said this is what I did and this is what it taught me. I realised that learning is only half the job. The other half is being able to show it. So I made a decision. From then on I wouldn’t just go through courses, I would finish them and earn the certificate at the end. Over a few months of vacation I worked through certified courses, one of which was a DSA in Python course by Jovial ML. It was a small change, from “I’m learning” to “I’m learning, and I can prove it.” But it was also the first time I started thinking about my future in a structured way, not as something that would just happen to me. SEM 4Stepping outside my own campus By the fourth semester, study, exams and submissions weren’t enough to fill my head. I wanted to see what else was out there. So I started participating in inter-college competitions, mostly coding contests and tech quizzes, while still keeping up with everything else college demanded. I took part in many and won a few, and yes, the wins felt great. But what actually changed was what I was chasing. I wanted to explore as many colleges around us as I could, walk into their events, talk to new students and build connections with people I’d never have met otherwise. Every competition was really an excuse to meet a new campus. Sketch of a medal with a star on blue and red ribbons, a small trophy cup, and sparkles { } ? coding contests & tech quizzes Fig. 3 — the semester I started collecting colleges. That was the semester I noticed my world was bigger than my college. Until then, “college” meant one building and the same faces. Suddenly it meant a whole city of students, all working through their own version of the same journey. SEM 4 · VACATIONThe internship we almost didn’t get At the end of that vacation came vocational training, and with it a lesson that wasn’t in any syllabus. We didn’t want to wait for a company to be handed to us. So my friend Anand and I decided to find one ourselves, by physically going everywhere we could. We covered the city and the industrial areas on a bike, on trips of 100+ km, marking every location on Google Maps as we went. At almost every stop the story ended in one of three ways: the place was closed, it didn’t offer internships, or it wanted our money. That third one was the pattern. Several places were happy to give us an “internship certificate” plus some training, for a fee. It was what many of our seniors and classmates had done, and it was starting to look like the only way in. After enough locked doors, I was almost ready to quit. Sketch of a map with a dotted bike route, three red crossed-out pins and one blue starred pin, and a small bicycle 100+ km by bike ✕ closed · ✕ no internships · ✕ “pay us first” · ★ open! Fig. 4 — the search map: three kinds of closed doors, and one open one. Anand wouldn’t let me. He’s my best friend and my classmate, and he suggested one last try: go back to the Software IT Park area one more time. So the two of us rode there again. And there it was: a startup called Modi Innovations Pvt Ltd, open at the very moment we walked up. We asked whether they could give us an internship, and we ended up talking directly to the head of the startup’s branch in the IT Park, Abhishek Sir. Sketch of IT park buildings with rows of windows and a small unit with an open sign IT PARK OPEN open. finally. the IT Park, and the one door that was open Fig. 5 — the IT Park, and the startup that was open. He said yes. We told him how much effort we’d put into the search, and how many places had offered us paid training instead. We were honest that most of our seniors and classmates had taken that route and that we’d been about to take it as a last option too. That’s when Abhishek Sir taught us something I still carry with me: An internship is learning while you work. If someone asks you to pay for doing their work, say no. If I ever ask you to pay, leave here too. — Abhishek Sir, as I remember it He also cleared up a misconception that scams quietly depend on. Some internships are paid, which means the company pays you. A lot of students hear “paid internship” and assume it means they have to pay, and that confusion is exactly what lets fake programs charge fees. We had been about to take the paid option as a last resort. Instead we left with a real internship, and a lesson that saved us from paying for something that should have been paying us. SEM 5From participating to organising If the fourth semester was about participating, the fifth was about organising. I was selected as the Event Manager of the department, which meant I stopped only showing up to events and started running them. I managed departmental events and helped build a magazine and a website for the committee. It’s a very different feeling to be the person an event depends on. You see the work behind the curtain, the parts nobody claps for, and you start to appreciate every event you ever attended as a spectator. My study approach changed too. I became more strategic and more serious about scoring well, with the intention of getting the best results I could, and I wanted to be seen by my teachers as someone who gave everything. I was doing everything possible: for the exams, for the events, for the impression I was leaving. SEM 5 · PEOPLEThe friendship I chose on purpose This semester also held one of the most memorable and thoughtful decisions of my life. Everyone knows friendship isn’t something you can force. It builds by itself with the people you match vibes with, share interests with and spend time around. But in the fifth semester, for the first time in my life, I picked a friendship on purpose. I looked at who I’d genuinely want to learn from, and then I tried to build the bond. His name was Shubham, a student from the Computer Engineering department, and the best student in his class. I was inspired by him, truly. So I started following his orbit: talking to him, sharing what I knew. And it turned out he was fascinated by my programming skills and technical knowledge, which gave us something to trade. Sketch of two friends facing each other with speech bubbles, and two arrows between them labelled study habits and code how do you study? me teach me HTML! Shubham study habits code Fig. 6 — habits one way, code the other. From him I learned how to prepare for exams, study better, score better and get noticed by teachers. He learned how to study collaboratively instead of competitively, along with programming fundamentals like HTML, Android and more. Shubham is still my best friend today. I didn’t abandon my old friends, not for a moment. I had simply started spending more of my time with Shubham and his roommates, people who took studying seriously, so my days drifted toward the Computer Engineering crowd and, for a while, away from my AIML classmates. It was a nice experience of drifting, one I chose with my eyes open. SEM 6No space for regrets The final semester was full of everything: activities, events, work, projects, laughs, mistakes, responsibilities, emotions, memories. Honestly it was more than I could comfortably carry, and still I went through almost all of it. My perspective this time was simple. This was the last semester, so I wanted to spend it to the fullest, with as many experiences as I could fit in, so there would be no room for “I wish I had” later. Sports, gatherings, events, final-year projects, and whatnot. I said yes to almost everything, and “almost” is where the best stories live. Sketch of a tilted carrom board with coins, a striker and a red queen, with notes about winning but having my name mispronounced we won! (the trophy part, anyway) but my name got mispronounced on stage. Fig. 7 — the carrom board, and the name that came out wrong. Not everything went perfectly, which is exactly why I remember it. A few moments from that semester: The carrom win I missed on stage I was part of the carrom team, and we won. But when the winners were called up, the speaker didn’t pronounce my name correctly, and in the confusion I missed my moment: walking up, taking the prize and shaking hands with the principal, the trustees and everyone else on stage. We won, and I still laugh about the one part I didn’t get to do. What carrom cost me The matches were scheduled on the same day as our cultural events, so I couldn’t attend many of the great things happening on campus. And then, to make it a little sadder, our teacher didn’t allow us to play the further interzonal matches, because our internal exams fell on the same day. The pani puri stall The day before the carrom matches was our traditional day, along with a funfair at college. My best friend Mayur had a pani puri stall, and as I was passing by, he pulled me in to help serve plates to a crowd that simply didn’t end. His stall won first prize, and I was genuinely happy for him. The catch: I’d spent the day behind the counter instead of in the photos, so I missed taking pictures with our classmates. He missed them too. The stage act I was also managing the art and design team for our department’s stage act, themed on Jammu & Kashmir. A few girls from the DDGM department worked under me to get everything done. Another responsibility, and another thing I’d never have done if I hadn’t said yes. None of those memories are perfect, and I wouldn’t trade a single imperfect one. I didn’t leave the last semester with a list of things I should have done. I left with a list of things I did, mispronounced name and missing photos included. LOOKING BACKWhat I took from it Put all six semesters in one place and the pattern is hard to miss. This is what my notebook margin would look like: Curiosity came first, then proof, then people, then leadership, then fullness. None of the shifts were planned. I only saw the pattern when I looked back. Each version of me was right for its semester, and each one made the next version possible. I’m sharing this because I feel many of you go through such mental shifts in your own journey. Your beliefs and your thinking about certain things change during these years, and it’s great to see it happen, to watch your mindset take shape along the way. If you’re in the middle of a semester right now: which version of you is it? Hope it was insightful. — Yash

title: Student of Life: Being a Continuous Learner
webpageTitle: Student of Life: Being a Continuous Learner — The Dev Notebook
dek: School & college taught us that learning is boring. Here’s why I’m choosing to unlearn that.
excerpt: Why I call myself a “Student of Life”: a hackathon story about learning by doing, why “I can’t” usually means “I haven’t yet,” and why learning shouldn’t stop when school does.
text: Student of Life: Being a Continuous Learner School & college taught us that learning is boring. Here’s why I’m choosing to unlearn that. Think about the word “learning.” What picture comes to your mind first? For most of us, it’s a classroom. A thick book. A pen running out of ink. An exam hall where everyone is quiet and nervous. 🏫 We spend many years in schools and colleges studying one subject after another, and somewhere along the way we quietly make a decision without noticing it: learning is boring work. Read it, write it, repeat it, take the test, forget it. We do all this without much interest, because we have to. I think this is one of the biggest things school gets wrong. Nobody teaches us this on purpose. It just slowly becomes a habit: learning equals boring. THE PROBLEMThe “only when it’s compulsory” trap 🙅‍♂️ The problem begins when the classroom ends. Once we link learning with boredom, we stop learning in our daily life. A new skill, a new tool, a new subject: our first answer is “no,” unless it becomes absolutely necessary. Until the deadline comes. Until the exam is tomorrow. Until the job asks for it. Waiting for a “must” before we learn is a poor way to live. Learning is the one skill that makes every other skill possible, and we treat it like a punishment. I didn’t understand how big this problem is until I saw it up close, in a place where there was no time to hide from it. THE STORYA hackathon, six people, and one restaurant ⏱️ It was around the even semester of my 2nd year of degree. Some of my old diploma friends from the Computer and IT department invited me to join their hackathon team. If you’ve never heard of one, a hackathon is a contest where teams build a working product in a very short time. Ours gave us 24 hours. One day, one night, and a list of requirements the judges would check at the end. Sketch of a stopwatch between a moon and a sun, with a checklist of ticked boxes beside it 24h one day, one night the judges’ list Fig. 1 — one day, one night, and a list to finish. We were a team of six, split into three pairs: two people on backend two people on frontend two people on ML (the “smart” part of the project) I was in the backend pair, along with Tanishq. The frontend pair was Harsh and Kartik. Here’s the easiest way to understand those roles. Imagine a restaurant: The frontend is the dining area. It’s what the customer sees: the menu, the tables, the look and feel. The backend is the kitchen. The real work happens there, and the customer never sees it. The “doors” between them, where the waiter takes an order to the kitchen and brings the food back, are called API endpoints. The ML side is like a clever chef who decides things using patterns and data. 🤖 Sketch of a restaurant: a dining table on the left labelled frontend, a kitchen with a pot and chef hat on the right labelled backend, and a serving window between them with arrows for orders and food dining area frontend order food kitchen backend ML chef the serving window = API endpoints Fig. 2 — frontend, backend, and the window between them. My job was to build the kitchen, which meant the endpoints and the connection to the database, where all our information was stored. Harsh and Kartik were good at the dining area. They built the screens of the app, and they did it well. THE WALLThe wall 🧱 Here’s where things got stuck. My kitchen was ready. I had given Harsh and Kartik everything they needed: the list of doors, and the details of how to knock on each one. In simple words, I had handed them the order form. But the dining area and the kitchen still weren’t talking to each other. They had never worked with a backend before, so they didn’t know how to send a request from their screens to my endpoints, get the data back and show it on the app. The hours were going by, and the clock was loud. Sketch of a phone on the left, a brick wall in the middle and a database on the right, with a dashed arrow from the phone stopping at the wall the wall screens ? the data Fig. 3 — everything was ready on both sides, but nothing could cross. I helped them, of course. We sat together and I walked them through it step by step until their screens finally started showing real data. The work got done. But I’ll be honest with you. I was a little annoyed. 😤 My feeling was not “why are you so slow?” It was closer to: you could have figured this out. The information was all there. The doors were listed, and the way to knock was explained. If they had tried, searched and experimented on their own, I could have spent that time building more of the backend, and helping Tanishq, who had his own hard problems. In a 24-hour contest, every hour I spent teaching was an hour I didn’t spend building. THE ONE WHO DID ITThe one who just did it 💪 And then there was Tanishq. Tanishq had no previous experience with the backend technology we were using. He also had no experience with React, which is the tool we used to build our real-time dashboard, the live screen that updates by itself as new information comes in. He had every right to say, “I’ve never done this, give it to someone else.” He didn’t say that. He sat down, figured it out, and built the backend work he had taken on and the whole real-time dashboard himself. Nobody had to hold his hand. Because of that, I had the room to focus on other parts of the project. That space is the real gift one person’s attitude gives the whole team. By the end of the 24 hours we had completed every requirement the judges had asked for. 🏆 THE LESSONNobody was wrong. Nobody was right. I want to be very clear about something, because I’ve thought about this for a long time: no one in this story was the bad guy. Harsh and Kartik are talented. Their frontend was good, and it’s exactly the kind of work that makes a project feel real. They weren’t lazy, and they weren’t careless. They simply weren’t in the habit of reaching beyond what they already knew, because for most of us, that was never encouraged. In school, we’re told to stay inside the syllabus. Tanishq wasn’t a genius either. He didn’t know more than they did when he started. He had the same blank start, the same unfamiliar tools and the same ticking clock. The only difference was his approach to learning: if I need it, I’ll learn it, right now. That’s the whole point of this post. It isn’t about who is better. It’s about which mindset we want to build in ourselves. THE HABIT“We can’t do this” 💻 I’ve seen smaller versions of this story many times among my friends. Someone learns a tech stack, a set of tools for building things. They get comfortable and stay inside it forever. Then a project needs something slightly different, or a simple task comes up that’s a step outside their comfort zone. And the answer is often: “We can’t do this.” Sketch of a hanging tag where the word can’t is crossed out and replaced by haven’t yet can’t haven’t yet same sentence, one small word Fig. 4 — “can’t” is almost always “haven’t yet.” But if you look closely, that sentence is almost never true. What they mean is “I haven’t done this yet.” And the gap between “can’t” and “haven’t yet” is usually much smaller than it looks. Often it’s a weekend of trying, a few tutorials and a couple of errors that make you want to throw your laptop. 🙃 Think about it: the people who build impressive things aren’t born knowing every tool. They’re just the ones who didn’t say no first. THE METHODThe best teacher is the thing itself 🔧 There’s a line I keep going back to. Someone once said: Actually doing a thing is the best way to learn it. 💯 — a line I keep coming back to I’ve found it true again and again. Reading about swimming doesn’t teach you to swim. Watching ten videos on cooking doesn’t make the dish taste right. We think we’ve understood something because it made sense while we were reading. But real understanding comes in the first moment something breaks and we have to fix it. Tanishq proved it to me. He wasn’t “ready” for that task. He became ready by doing it. And honestly, so did every one of us at that hackathon, in different ways. So I believe we should be able to adapt to whatever comes our way. If we need to learn something new, or work with a technology we’ve never touched, we should do it without hesitation. Not because it’s easy, but because that’s how we grow. 🌱 THE DESKThe desk where it happens Since we’re talking about doing, here’s my corner. This is my desk at the hostel, with a new cup from GDGC added to it. ☕ Photo of my hostel desk with few post-its attached for me my hostel desk, and few post-its It’s not fancy. But it’s where a lot of my “I’ll figure it out” moments happen. THE WHYNot just for marks. Not just for jobs. 🧠 So what is the point of learning, if not for good marks or a good job? Let me be honest: those are real reasons, and I’m not going to pretend otherwise. We all want to do well, and we all need to earn. There’s nothing wrong with that. But if those are the only reasons, then something strange happens. The moment the exam is over, we stop learning. The moment the job is secured, we stop growing. We end up using a tiny part of what we’re capable of, and we call it “enough.” That’s why my mindset is simple: I want to learn things, but not only to score high, and not only to get hired. I want to learn because understanding things makes life bigger. Because there’s a quiet joy in being able to say, “I couldn’t do this last month, and now I can.” ✨ THE IDENTITYWhy my profile says “Student of Life” 🎓 If you’ve seen my LinkedIn, you may have noticed that I describe myself as a Student of Life. Screenshot of my LinkedIn profile showing the headline Student of Life where it says it: Student of Life I wrote that on purpose, and I mean it fully. I believe we should remain students for our whole life. Not just in technical skills, but in every area: experiencing new things, trying new things, being a beginner again and again. Cooking, music, philosophy, a new language, how to handle people, how to handle ourselves. 💫☀️ Being a beginner doesn’t feel great. You look clumsy. You make mistakes. You can’t skip the awkward part. But it’s the only road that leads anywhere new. And the good news is that you don’t need a classroom for any of it. You don’t need permission, and you don’t need an exam at the end. All you need is curiosity, and the willingness to say “let me try.” Sketch of a graduation cap with a tassel resting on a pencil a lifelong student Fig. 5 — the cap goes on once. The pencil stays in hand. BEFORE YOU GOOne small word Next time you hear yourself say “I can’t do this,” pause for a second and add one small word at the end: “I can’t do this… yet.” Then open the tool, read the first page, break the first thing and fix it. You’ll be surprised how fast “can’t” turns into “I did.” You should be a lifelong learner. You should be a lifelong student. 🎓 — Yash

title: Chasing Perfection: Why I Know Better and Still Can’t Stop
webpageTitle: Chasing Perfection: Why I Know Better and Still Can’t Stop — The Dev Notebook
dek: On doing things with intention, getting stuck anyway, and what I’m learning along the way.
excerpt: Why I keep chasing perfection even when I know it drains me: the perfect 3D portfolio I never built, the normal one I made in a week, and three lessons about focus, small steps and pushing limits.
text: Chasing Perfection: Why I Know Better and Still Can’t Stop On doing things with intention, getting stuck anyway, and what I’m learning along the way. Here’s a small confession from someone who tracks his expenses, his screen time and his schedule: I know that chasing perfection is not always a good idea. I’ve read the books. I can explain the theory. I could probably give a short talk on it. ⚡ And yet, when I sit down to do something, I still catch myself spending far too long trying to do it perfectly. It takes time. It drains my energy. Sometimes it leaves me mentally stuck, staring at one small detail while the rest of the work waits. And even after all that, letting go is hard. I want to write about this honestly, because I think many of you know this feeling, even if you call it something else. THE CONFESSIONI know. I still do it. 🔁 Knowing something and doing it are very different things, and perfectionism is the best example I have. You rewrite one sentence five times. You fix the alignment of something nobody else will ever notice. You delay starting because the plan isn’t perfect yet. The work isn’t finished, but it feels like work, so it feels okay. ⌚ Sketch of a page with the same sentence written and crossed out three times, next to a pencil whose eraser is almost gone draft 1: the same sentence draft 2: the same sentence draft 3: the same sentence draft 4: still not right… the eraser is almost gone Fig. 1 — one sentence, many drafts. The funny part is that I’m often trying to save time. I plan carefully, I organise, I want to avoid mistakes so I won’t have to redo things later. But perfectionism quietly takes back every hour I was trying to save. THE REAL ISSUEIt’s not really about being flawless Here’s something I had to figure out slowly: for me, this isn’t about wanting to be flawless, or wanting everyone to clap. It’s the deep urge to do things with intention. With care. With precision. I want my work to feel like it was made by someone who meant it, and that’s a good thing. Caring about quality is not the problem. The problem starts when “doing it with care” quietly becomes “I can’t stop until it’s perfect.” Those two feel almost the same from the inside, but they lead to very different places. Care says: “Let me do this well.” Perfectionism says: “Let me not do this until I can’t fail.” — note to self The first one moves you forward. The second one keeps you standing still. THE STORYThe portfolio that never got built 🕹️ The best example I have of this is my portfolio. For almost a quarter of a year, I was going to build the perfect one. Notice the wording: not building, going to build. It started with something beautiful. I’d come across portfolios like Bruno Simon’s, and a few others, which aren’t websites in the usual sense. They’re small 3D worlds built with Three.js. You move around inside them, play with the animations, and while you play, you slowly find out who the person is, what they’ve made and what they care about. It felt like a game that happened to be a resume. I was hooked. That’s the one I want. Sketch comparing a browser window containing a 3D cube world, labelled the dream, with a plain browser page of cards, labelled the real one vs the dream: a whole 3D world the real one: plain, but finished Fig. 2 — the portfolio I imagined, and the one I actually needed. So I planned everything. Then, one by one, the obstacles showed up: To make the 3D models, I had to learn Blender. To bring them to life, I had to get much better at Three.js. To run Blender properly, I needed a powerful PC, and I don’t have one. And all of it needed a lot, lot of time. I treated each of these as a gate I had to pass before I could start. So I spent days figuring out how to build 3D models, watching tutorials, researching and “preparing”. I felt busy. I felt serious. Planning feels like progress, which is exactly why it’s so dangerous. Meanwhile, I had a bigger roadmap in my head, and of course it was perfect: Build a cool portfolio. Make a resume. Hunt for internships. Be working, and getting paid, within a month or two. Then life got in the way. Hackathons. SIH (the Smart India Hackathon, a big national contest). Tests. Submissions. Regular classes. Home visits during vacations. Festivals. Every one of them was worth doing, and every one of them pushed my plan a little further away. Sketch of a calendar grid filled with tests, SIH, classes, hackathons, festivals and home visits, with a single empty box labelled portfolio the quarter tests SIH classes hackathon home festival submit classes tests home festival classes SIH submit portfolio? life, happening Fig. 3 — every box was worth filling, and none of them was the portfolio. When I finally finished everything else and sat down to get back to the portfolio, I noticed something uncomfortable. Nothing was built. No pages, no models, nothing. After all that time, what I had was a plan. I’d been busy designing the perfect portfolio, and I hadn’t made one. THE TURNThe thing I learned the hard way 🎯 Around then I watched a lot of videos about how a portfolio should look and how to build one. And one thing kept showing up. I’m applying for game programming roles. A recruiter looking at someone like me isn’t going to care how magical my website’s 3D world is. Honestly, they’d barely notice it. I looked at the other people in my space who were applying, and most of them had pretty normal portfolios. What set them apart was what was inside: the projects, and the thinking behind them. The dream version of my portfolio was built for me, and not for the people who’d be reading it. I won’t pretend that was easy to accept. Dropping the idea took a lot of courage. I’d spent so long imagining it that letting go felt like admitting the time was wasted. But it was the first useful thing I’d done in months. So I started over with a normal portfolio. It’s not the best or the nicest one out there. But it’s the one recruiters will actually see, and the one that shows what matters. I built it in less than a week. Bar chart: one very tall bar for almost a quarter of a year of planning with nothing live, and one tiny bar for less than a week of building that is live almost a quarter of a year, and nothing live less than a week, and it’s live ✓ planning the perfect one building the real one Fig. 4 — the same me, with two very different approaches. Think about that for a second: almost a quarter of a year for a portfolio that never existed, and less than a week for one that does. 🤯 The perfect portfolio never went live. The normal one did. THE COSTWhat it costs me ⚖️ Let me be honest about the price of this habit, with that story fresh in mind: Time. In my case, a full quarter of a year, and a lot of small hours before that. Energy. I finish tired, even when I haven’t done much new work. Starting. Sometimes I don’t begin at all, because the first step won’t be perfect. Peace. Even when something is good, I’m already thinking about what’s wrong with it. And the strangest part is that perfectionism can make me feel productive while keeping me stuck. Planning and polishing are easier than finishing, because finishing means somebody might see it. THE SHIFTSo I try to shift my focus 🧭 Different experiences on this journey have taught me that chasing perfection alone is exhausting. So I’m trying something else. Instead of asking, “Is this perfect?” I ask, “Does this reflect me?” I put more effort into building something that shows my thoughts, my values and my journey. My normal portfolio does that far better than my dream one ever could, because it’s mine and it’s real. It’s honest. That’s a much better thing to chase, because I can actually reach it. THE DIFFERENCERespect is slower than recognition 🤝 I’ve also noticed something about people. Recognition is quick. A flashy design, a good result, a good post, and people say “wow.” But it fades just as fast. Respect is different. It’s earned slowly, and it comes from doing things with honesty and discipline, again and again, even when nobody is watching. A 3D world might get a “wow” once. Clear projects and honest thinking get trust for years. I’d rather earn that. THE CYCLELearning, unlearning, and starting again 🧠 Along the way I’ve had to unlearn a lot: old habits, limiting beliefs and even outdated ways of thinking that I carried without noticing. “A portfolio must be amazing” was one of them. I used to think learning was a one-time thing: you learn something and it’s yours forever. But it’s more like a cycle: Pick up a new idea. Let go of what you no longer need. Start again, with an open mind. It’s tough, because letting go of an old belief feels like losing a part of yourself. But it’s freeing too. Every time I drop a rule that wasn’t helping me, I find I have more room to breathe. THREE LESSONSThree things I learned along the way 📌 These are the lessons I keep coming back to. I think they’ll be useful to you too. LESSON 1Pay attention to what truly matters 🎯 There’s always a lot going on around us: distractions, other people’s opinions, things pulling us in different directions. It’s easy to spend a whole day busy and still feel like nothing important got done. That’s why it’s so important to decide what truly matters to us. We don’t have endless time or energy, so we should spend both on the things that actually help us grow or bring us peace. Sketch of a compass whose red needle points to the words what matters, surrounded by distractions like noise, opinions, trends and maybe later what matters noise opinions maybe later trends Fig. 5 — a lot is pulling at us. The needle still has to point somewhere. My portfolio is a clear example. What mattered was the projects and the thinking behind them. I was spending my energy on 3D models. Perfectionism spreads our care evenly over everything. Focus puts it where it counts. LESSON 2Small steps, every single day 🔮 Getting better doesn’t always mean doing something big. Even small improvements, done every day, can make a big difference over time. It might not show up right away, but it adds up, slowly and surely. The key is to keep going, even on days when we don’t feel like it. Sketch of a staircase of six steps labelled day 1 to day 6 with a small figure climbing and a flag at the top day 1 day 2 day 3 day 4 day 5 day 6 an okay day, repeated Fig. 6 — nobody climbs it in one jump. What shapes our future isn’t only how talented we are. It’s how patient and consistent we stay, even when it’s tough. A perfect day happens once in a while. An okay day, repeated a hundred times, builds a life. And a simple site built in a week beats a perfect one that was never started. LESSON 3Push past the limits you didn’t know you set 🏆 We set limits for ourselves, sometimes without even realising it. “I’m not good at this.” “That’s for other people.” “Maybe later.” We should try to push past those limits. Go after goals that feel a bit scary or out of reach. That’s usually where real growth begins: in the moments we step out of our comfort zone and try something that challenges us. You might think this clashes with everything I said about the portfolio, but I don’t think it does. Dreaming big was never the mistake. The mistake was turning the dream into a condition for starting. A big goal is fine. Waiting for perfect conditions before you take the first step is what stops us. Perfection says “don’t try until you can’t fail.” Growth says “try, and learn from the failing.” I’m choosing the second. LAST WORDKeep the spark. Stay humble. 🏁 As we move forward, I think we should keep that spark alive: always wanting to learn more, try new things and grow. At the same time, we need to stay humble and remind ourselves that we don’t know everything yet, and that’s okay. It’s easy to get comfortable. It’s easy to stop aiming higher once things are going fine. But deep down, we know we can do more and be more. A normal portfolio built in a week beats a perfect one that never exists. So don’t settle for less than what you’re truly capable of, and don’t wait until it’s perfect to begin. 🏁 — Yash

title: “Bhaiya, Are You Yash Bhavsar?”: My First Talk to My Juniors
webpageTitle: “Bhaiya, Are You Yash Bhavsar?”: My First Talk to Juniors — The Dev Notebook
dek: A stranger in the hostel, a long night of thinking, and a talk that took me out of my comfort zone.
excerpt: How a junior’s question at my hostel became my first guidance talk for first-year AIML and CO students: the nerves, the blank moment, what I told them about learning online, and why the only way past the fear of speaking is to face it.
text: “Bhaiya, Are You Yash Bhavsar?”: My First Talk to My Juniors A stranger in the hostel, a long night of thinking, and a talk that took me out of my comfort zone. About a year ago, in my final year of diploma, I stood in front of a class of first-year students and gave a talk. 🎙 I wrote a short post about it on LinkedIn back then, while the feeling was still fresh. But I wanted the full story to live here, in my notebook, so here it is. One more thing before we start: I gave this talk in Marathi, our own language, so that everyone in the room could follow it easily. In this post I’ve translated everything into English, so it’s understandable to everyone. 🏫 THE INVITATIONA question in the hostel 😅 It began on an ordinary day, I was visiting in the hostel. A group of juniors was passing by. I didn’t know any of them. Then one of them stopped, turned and asked: “Bhaiya, are you Yash Bhavsar?” Sketch of a hostel corridor with doors, a junior with a speech bubble asking Bhaiya, are you Yash Bhavsar, and a confused figure on the left ? “Bhaiya, are you Yash Bhavsar?” a junior me, confused Fig. 1 — the question that started it all. I said yes, a bit confused. He told me that he and some of his classmates had seen my profile on LinkedIn, and they’d even shown it to their teacher. They had liked it so much that they wanted to invite me to their class, to give some guidance to the first-year students. I didn’t know what to say. Nobody had ever asked me anything like that. It took me a moment just to digest the question, let alone the request. So I did the only thing I could: I told him I’d let him know in a day or two, and we exchanged contacts. His name was Arjun. THE DECISIONThe night I couldn’t stop thinking 🌙 Back in my room, I couldn’t think about anything else. I talked it over with Anand, my best friend and the same friend who’d ridden with me across the city looking for an internship. The more I thought about it, the clearer it became: this was exactly the kind of opportunity I’d always wanted. I’ve always been inspired by people who give talks: TED talks, famous speeches, all of it. I’d given a few speeches myself back in my school days, but they were for events like Teachers’ Day and Independence Day. In every one of them, I told the stories of people from the past who had won in life. I had never told my own story. I write my stories in LinkedIn posts and in my journal, but standing on a stage and saying them out loud was something I’d honestly love to do. And that’s where the real challenge sat. I’m an introvert, someone who fears speaking even a word in a crowd. Developing the courage to go there was the hard part, much more than the talk itself. But I decided. I called Arjun and said: “Yes. I’ll be there next week.” THE SCRIPTWhat do I even say? 📝 Once I knew I’d do it, my head filled up with questions: What could I tell them? How should I start? What’s actually useful for a first-year student? And what if I say something wrong? I thought about it a lot. It was really hard for me, because I overthink everything, and this was a talk about my own story, which made it feel even more personal. I was also deep in practicals and other work at the time, so free time was tight. Still, I finalised the date, and then I did what I always do when I’m unsure: I wrote everything down. I prepared a script for the talk. Sketch of a script page with two crossed-out opening lines and one kept opening, surrounded by worried questions Hi everyone, today I will… Good morning juniors, so… Hello Friends! what do I say? how do I start? what if I get it wrong? what’s useful? ? Fig. 2 — the script, and the questions around it. THE NERVESThe nerves before the door Even with the script, I was nervous before I went. What if I miss something? What if I forget an important point? What if nobody reacts? It’s a strange feeling. You know the topic because it’s your own journey, and still your heart doesn’t believe you. THE MOMENTThen I walked in 😬 I started a little scared. I picked up a piece of chalk and wrote a few words on the board, in my worst handwriting, so messy that even I couldn’t understand it. Then I turned and looked at the whole class, and I went blank. I just started speaking the words I had crammed, in a brittle, under-confident voice. The teacher noticed, and told me to relax. I took a deep breath, closed my eyes for a split second, and told myself: Yash, you can do it. — me, to me, with my eyes closed And then I faced it. Sketch of a blackboard with unreadable scribbles and a chalk piece, and a small face with closed eyes thinking Yash, you can do it (even I can’t read it) Yash, you can do it… Fig. 3 — messy chalk, a deep breath, and one sentence to myself. THE RELIEFAnd then it went really well ✔ Everything after that went good. I asked them a few questions, which were part of my script. They asked a few doubts too, and I was able to solve them. The students were interested, they stayed engaged, and by the end it was a really nice, interactive session. 🎓 It wasn’t a lecture, it was a conversation. And it was much better than the version my nerves had imagined. THE TALKWhat I told them Here’s what I actually shared, translated from the script. My topic was online courses. But I didn’t want to talk about which courses to take. I wanted to talk about why we should do courses at all, and why online learning matters. THE TALK · OPENERI started with a question Before the topic, I asked them something: You all came to diploma after your 10th. Some of you came just because your parents said so. Some of you came with a dream. It could be anything: a web developer, a software developer. Can two or three of you tell me what your dream is, and why you chose diploma? A few students shared theirs. Mostly the kinds of dreams I expected: data scientist, web developer, and so on. THE TALK · MY REASONA lockdown, a game and a YouTube search 🎮 Then I told them about my first day in first year. In the very first lecture, our English madam asked everyone to introduce themselves and say what their dream was. I said I wanted to be a game developer. I told them that behind every dream there should be a reason. The reason can be anything, but it has to be there. If you want to be a web developer only because your friend is becoming one, or because the job pays well, it will be very hard to survive in this field. So I told them my reason. During the lockdown, we were all at home with no school and no studies. Like many others, I was just passing time, mostly playing Free Fire. Months went by like that. But as my 10th boards came closer, something inside me said, this has to stop. Sketch of a game controller on the left, an arrow, and a code window on the right showing a code symbol </> just passing time “how are games made?” Fig. 4 — from playing games to wondering how they’re made. So I asked myself a different question: what do I actually like? And I realised I was curious about how games are made. I started searching on YouTube. That’s how I learned that programming languages exist, and that one of them, C#, can be used to make games. That’s also when I understood that “game developer” is an actual career path. I was honest with them about what happened next. I learned some C# before my final boards, but there was a gap of 3 to 4 months and I forgot most of it. The language was also tricky, and I couldn’t find a good tutorial, so my programming basics never became clear. After my 10th, during the vacation, I kept exploring. That’s when I found CodeWithHarry’s Python course and followed it. From there, my interest in programming kept growing. By the time I took admission to diploma, I had already learned Python, C, C++ and Data Structures, only by watching those tutorials. THE TALK · THE GAPWhy college alone isn’t enough I told them that everything I’d learned before diploma is something they would also learn in their three years of diploma, and later in degree. But college teaching is mostly at the theory level. We study subjects for the paper, and once the final exam is over, we forget most of it. And when we go into the industry, our skills matter far more than our degree or diploma certificate. You can’t learn how real software is built by writing code on a notebook page. That’s why I told them to focus on online learning alongside college. THE TALK · CLASSESAbout paid classes Many students join classes: M1, M2, C, Java and many more. But I often hear that even in those classes, the teaching is mostly theoretical. I told them that personally, I never joined classes during my diploma, because I never needed to. Most of what classes charge for is available online for free, on YouTube and on many other platforms. I wasn’t saying “don’t join classes.” That’s your choice. I only asked them to think about this: if you used that same time on an online course, how much could you gain? THE TALK · FOUR RULESFour things that improve your skills Of course, following online courses doesn’t mean following every course you find. I told them four things matter. Four sketched cards numbered one to four: a lightbulb for curiosity, a loop for practice, a cube for projects and a branching graph for up to date technology 1 2 3 4 explore curiosity practice by doing build projects stay up to date four things, one direction Fig. 5 — the four points from my script. RULE 1Explore your curiosity You have two to three years. It feels like a lot, but it passes quickly. If you try to explore everything, time will run out and you’ll learn nothing completely. So learn what makes you curious. In my case, I wanted to be a game developer, but I was also interested in Android and web development, so I explored those too. Some of my friends are interested in cyber security and IoT hardware, so they explore those. You could even plan it semester by semester: web development this semester, data science the next. By the end, you’d have explored three or four fields. Some friends tell me I’m giving the wrong advice, that you should learn only the field you want a career in. But my view is that in industry, whether you’re applying for a job or starting your own startup, it’s expected that you know a little about every field. RULE 2Practice by doing Say you’re watching a four-hour tutorial series. Do you watch all four hours in one day? It’s not a movie. Watching it all at once doesn’t mean you’ve learned it. You need real practice. Run what the video teaches on your own computer. Change something and see how the output changes. Many people think coding is just writing programs, but coding is really problem solving: how you think through a problem, and how you turn those steps into a program. Programming languages are mostly similar, and only the syntax, the way of writing, changes. Once your problem-solving mindset develops, you can write code in any language. Picking up a language can take about a day. Learning to solve problems takes much longer, and the more you practise, the faster you learn. RULE 3Build projects Writing small programs is good practice, but it doesn’t mean you now know coding. You also need to understand how a small piece of code works inside a large system, and what happens to a whole website or app if there’s a small mistake in it. You only learn that by building projects. You don’t have to build everything on your own at the start. If you don’t know how to build a project, follow an online tutorial and code along with it. You’ll still learn a lot, and later, you’ll get ideas for projects of your own. And the projects you build yourself are worth a lot in industry. In interviews, they ask what projects you’ve made and how you made them. If you built them yourself, you have a clear advantage. RULE 4Learn up-to-date technologies The last point: stay updated with new technologies. A lot is going on around AI right now. There are AI tools that can build an entire website without you writing any code, so you should at least know such tools exist. You’ll also see ads saying “Become an AI Expert for ₹99” or “Become an AI Master.” Don’t fall for them. Professors from places like Harvard and Stanford, who know far more than the people selling those courses, have their courses available for free on YouTube and other platforms. And one more thing: when you learn technologies, first learn Git and GitHub. It’s a version control system. It lets you maintain versions of your software, and it records who changed what in the code, and when. THE TALK · THE ENDHow I ended At the end, I told them I’d send a PDF with all the online learning platforms and courses I know, so they could explore them. It would also include the courses I’ve done myself, in case they wanted to know. Then I thanked Mahamuni Sir for giving me the chance to speak to them, genuinely, from the heart. And I told the students: if you have any questions, ask without any hesitation. LOOKING BACKWhy this one was different I’ve done speeches, seminar presentations and project presentations before. A guidance talk was new for me. In a seminar or project presentation, you show your work and someone judges it. In a guidance talk, nobody is checking your slides. You’re sharing your own experience and trusting people with it, and what you say could change how someone spends their next three years. That’s a different kind of responsibility, and a different kind of nervous. 🙂 LOOKING BACK“Invited while still in college” 🎇 I listen to many people online. A common story goes like this: they finish college, become successful in life, and then get invited back to give a talk at their own college. Mine happened earlier. I was invited while I was still in college, in my final year. And honestly, I feel really proud of that. 🎇 I don’t say this to brag. It showed me that you don’t need to wait until you’re “successful” for your experience to be useful. It’s useful the moment you’ve learned something that someone else is still trying to learn. THE FEARThe fear of public speaking 😬 Like many people, I fear public speaking. The fast heartbeat, the dry mouth, the feeling that everyone is judging you. I get all of it. Sketch of a heartbeat line that is sharp and spiky on the left and becomes a calm smooth wave on the right after a deep breath one deep breath walking in a few minutes later Fig. 6 — the fear didn’t vanish. It just got smaller. And the only thing that has ever really worked is this: the only way to overcome the fear is to face it. Not reading about it, not planning for it, not waiting until you feel ready. Facing it, one real room at a time. The fear didn’t disappear when I walked in. It just got smaller than my willingness to do it. TAKEAWAYSWhat I took from it 📌 Share your journey, even when it feels small. This invitation came because students found my LinkedIn profile. I never posted to get invited. I shared what I was learning, and someone found it useful. Let preparation give your nerves somewhere to go. The script didn’t remove my nervousness, but it gave it a direction. Say yes to the room that scares you. Every time I’ve faced a fear, it was smaller than the version in my head. If there’s a talk, a presentation or a room that scares you, I hope this nudges you towards it. Be nervous. Do it anyway. 👍 I hope you gained something from it. — Yash

title: Workless Days Are Reflection Days
webpageTitle: Workless Days Are Reflection Days — The Dev Notebook
dek: No laptop, a long family function and a half-finished to-do list. Here’s what I did with the time.
excerpt: A trip to Nashik, a long traditional function and a paper journal: why days when you can’t work are reflection days, with six prompts from an Ali Abdaal video to try on yours.
text: Workless Days Are Reflection Days No laptop, a long family function and a half-finished to-do list. Here’s what I did with the time. There will be some days when you won’t be able to work. 💼👨‍💻 I know that sounds obvious. But if you’re someone who tracks everything, plans everything and wants to progress every single day, as I do, you know how heavy those days can feel. THE TRIPThe trip to Nashik 🚂🧳 A year or two ago, I travelled to Nashik to visit my didi’s home. She’s my cousin: my father’s sister’s daughter. We went by train, and we stayed for 3 to 4 days. Sketch of a train with two carriages and an engine puffing smoke along a track, heading to Nashik → Nashik 3–4 days, one journal, no laptop Fig. 1 — the train to Nashik, with no project in the bag. The reason for the visit was a Vastu Shanti, a traditional ritual performed at a new home. It was a long family function, the kind with a lot of waiting, a lot of rituals and a lot of people talking. And honestly, I’ll admit it: this isn’t the kind of event I usually bother much about. 😅 I didn’t bring my laptop. So there was no project to open, no code to write, nothing to push to GitHub. I had only one thing with me: a paper journal. THE GUILTDoing nothing, loudly 🤒 When you’re used to being busy, doing nothing is not quiet. It’s loud. I sat there, free, and my brain started listing everything I could have been doing instead: the projects I’d left half done, the courses I’d started and stopped, the things I’d told myself I would finish “soon.” Sketch of a person sitting still, surrounded by thought bubbles about half-done projects, unfinished courses and wasting time half-done projects courses left halfway this is wasted time… doing nothing is loud Fig. 2 — a quiet function, and a very noisy head. The more I thought about it, the more it felt like I was wasting time. The guilt arrived, the same guilt I get on any day I can’t progress. We all carry a quiet rule in our heads: I should move forward every single day. But life doesn’t follow that rule. Sometimes it’s travel. Sometimes it’s sickness. Sometimes it’s a function, an event or a family occasion. 📆 THE PAUSEThen I opened the journal 📖 At some point, I took out the journal. I didn’t plan a big session. I just started writing about what was going on in my life, and how I could make it better. A few minutes turned into a few hours, just me, a pen and the page. Sketch of an open journal with handwriting asking what is working and what is not, and a pen resting on the right page what’s working? what’s not? truths about me: 1. 2. 3. Fig. 3 — a few minutes became a few hours. And something shifted. I stopped seeing these days as lost days. I started seeing them as a pause: a chance to step back from day-to-day work, look at all the progress I’d already made, and ask where I was heading. Around then, I remembered an Ali Abdaal video about prompts for reflecting on your life. So I sat down and wrote my way through them. ✍️ THE SHIFTWhat if workless days are reflection days? 🌠 That day gave me a new way to treat these days. Think of them as reflection days. Sketch of a week of seven boxes: two work days ticked, four shaded pause days grouped under a bracket labelled reflection days, and one more ticked work day day 1 day 2 day 3 day 4 day 5 day 6 day 7 pause pause pause pause reflection days, not lost days Fig. 4 — the pause is part of the week, not a hole in it. If you can’t move forward, you can still look around. Instead of using the day to feel bad, ask honest questions: Were we doing our best? Were we spending time wisely across every aspect of life, not only work? Is there anything left behind? These are the questions we never have time for when we’re busy. A workless day gives us the time. 😇 THE PROMPTSThe prompts from that video ✍️ These are the prompts I worked through. They come from Ali Abdaal’s video, and you can try them on any workless day: 1. The Work Audit When it comes to work right now, what’s working and what’s not working? 2. The Life Audit When it comes to my life right now, what’s working and what’s not working? 3. The Truths Exercise What are 10 things that are true about you? 4. Fulfillment Stories Think about a time in your life when you did something well and it brought you a sense of fulfillment. 5. The Energy Audit Look back on your calendar or the activities you’ve done in the last two weeks and identify which ones gave you energy and which ones drained your energy. 6. Truth Statements What are some truths that you’d like to be true about yourself 12 months from now? You don’t have to answer them all. Pick one. Write for ten minutes. See what comes out. My favourites are the two audits, because they ask a simple question: what’s working and what’s not? It’s amazing how rarely we stop to ask it. Most of the time we just keep doing what we’ve always done and hope it works. Sketch of two batteries: one full with a lightning bolt labelled gave me energy, and one almost empty labelled drained me the energy audit gave me energy drained me Fig. 5 — two weeks of a calendar, sorted into full and empty. The Energy Audit is a good one for people like me, who track everything. It uses something we already keep, our calendar, and turns it into a question: which of these things gave me energy, and which ones drained it? 📋 The full PDF with all the prompts: open it on Google Drive → THE HOW-TOHow to spend a workless day ❤️ You don’t have to turn it into a task. Some things that help: Spend time with yourself. A walk, a window seat, a journal. Spend time with family. Be where you are, with the people you came to see. Let the day feel good. If it’s boring or guilty, you won’t reflect well. And try to watch your life from a detached perspective, like someone looking at a story from the outside. How is it going? What’s working? What isn’t? Sketch of a person standing on top of a hill looking at a small window showing their work, with a sun in the sky my work, from a distance Fig. 6 — a little distance makes it easier to see. When you look at things from a distance, you come back to your work with a positive vibe and fresh energy. ⚡🙌 A rested mind often solves in ten minutes what a tired mind couldn’t solve in two hours. THE TWISTThe unexpected part 🌱 I went to Nashik for a function I wasn’t excited about, with no laptop, no plan and no progress to show. And yet it turned out to be time well used, because it was one of the few times I’d sat still long enough to listen to myself. So if you have a day coming up when you can’t work, don’t dread it. 👇 BEFORE YOU GOSo make your workless days better 👍 Let it go. A few missed days won’t break your progress. Pause. Don’t fill the gap with guilt. Reflect. Pick a prompt, grab a notebook, and write. Return fresh. Start again with a clear head. Progress isn’t only the days we work. It’s also the days we step back, look at where we’re heading, and decide to keep going. 🌠 I hope it helps. 👍 — Yash

title: The Hackathon That Taught Me How Hard It Is to Lead Friends
webpageTitle: The Hackathon That Taught Me How Hard It Is to Lead Friends — The Dev Notebook
dek: A month of sleepless nights, six very different friends, and what SIH taught me about leading a team.
excerpt: My Smart India Hackathon story: choosing a problem statement, six friends with six different goals, conflicts, sleepless nights, and what I learned about leading a team that doesn’t share your dream.
text: The Hackathon That Taught Me How Hard It Is to Lead Friends A month of sleepless nights, six very different friends, and what SIH taught me about leading a team. The Smart India Hackathon, or SIH, is one of the most memorable experiences of my whole college life. It taught me things about myself, my friends and the bond between us that nothing else ever has. It’s also the hardest story I’ve written on this blog. It has conflicts, hurt feelings, headaches, long nights, and a lot of love tangled in between. I’ve tried to tell it exactly as it happened, including the uncomfortable parts. THE WISHA wish, and a promise to myself 🎯 In my third year of degree, I had one wish: to win a hackathon with my own classmates, and to be the one who led the winning team. This wasn’t my first hackathon. I’d been through a few, and I’d even won a prize at one with my old diploma friends at PICT, where we took 2nd place. To me, a 2nd prize still counts as a victory. But in that team I was one member among six. This time I wanted to do it myself, with people I studied with every day. I believed we had what it took. We had talent. We had the opportunity. All we needed was the right amount of effort to make it pay off. I had also been part of SIH in my second year, in a team of Harshada, Deep, Vinay, Mahesh, Sharayu and me. That time I didn’t like our project, because it wasn’t clear or unique enough for me to believe in. So this time, we decided to do things differently. THE EXPLAINERHow SIH works? (for readers outside our world) SIH is a national hackathon. Teams choose a problem statement (PS) from an official portal, a real-world problem posted by an organisation, and build a solution for it. It has three phases: Internal hackathon. This takes place at college, where every team presents to judges. The best teams are nominated. PPT screening. Nominated teams submit a presentation on the official SIH portal. Each team can submit at most two decks, on different problem statements, to improve their chances: if one doesn’t get selected, the other might, depending on how many submissions that problem statement receives. Only 5 out of about 500 decks per problem statement are selected. That’s roughly a 1% chance, and honestly, it’s the hardest phase of all. Grand Finale. The five selected teams per problem statement compete in a 24-hour physical hackathon, and 1 or 2 winners are picked. Sketch of a funnel of three bars: internal hackathon, PPT screening where 5 of about 500 decks are chosen, and the grand finale 1 · internal hackathon, at college 2 · PPT screening: 5 of ~500 3 · Grand Finale ~1% chance 24 hours, in person Fig. 1 — the funnel. The narrowest part is the one in the middle. THE CALMThe calm I wanted to learn 😌 Before I tell you about SIH, I have to tell you about PICT. That was the 24-hour hackathon I wrote about in Student of Life. I was there with my diploma friends Tanishq, Harsh and Kartik, and two new people, Pratik and Suhani, both former SIH winners. I was very tense. Nothing was fully working, and time was running out. But Pratik handled the entire team beautifully. He was so relaxed and calm that we were a little worried about him. And then, at the time of the presentation and explanation, he was the one who impressed the judges and took us to 2nd place. I came away deeply impressed. Not by his skills, but by his attitude towards the team and the project. I told myself: I want to be like that. THE RESEARCHThe research phase 🔍 For SIH, we did our homework properly. We went through every problem statement on the portal, one by one, with the pros and cons of choosing each. We did all the normal things a hackathon needs: picking a PS, understanding its requirements, building our approach, prototyping the solution, and so on. But one thing almost always gets missed, and it has the biggest effect on success: team bonding. I learned this the hard way. You can watch any number of YouTube videos on how to win SIH. They’ll teach you how to pick the best problem statement and how to make the best presentation. But nobody teaches you how to lead a team of friends. THE TEAMThe team 👥 I led a team of five others: Vinay, Sharayu, Mahesh, Harshada and Pranav. Honestly, this wasn’t the most skilled team in college. But it was the best I could get. Sharayu and Harshada had both received offers to join other teams, and they chose to stay, because they felt leaving wouldn’t be good for our friendship. I had also asked Tejas, a friend from the IT department and a very skilled developer. But he’d already built his own team. (That’s a different story. He’d asked me a few times in the past to join hackathons with him, and I’d always refused with some flimsy excuse about not having time. So it was only natural that he didn’t ask me this time.) This is who I ended up with: Sketch of six people in a row, each with a small label: ML, frontend, mood, magic voice, jack of all trades, and backend ML models frontend mood-based magic voice all-rounder backend Vinay Sharayu Mahesh Harshada Pranav me Fig. 2 — six people, six very different strengths. Vinay The best of us in ML, training models and AI development, but the weakest at presentation and explanation. Sharayu Good enough at presenting, fair at frontend and web design. Mahesh A little into backend design, good at thinking and decision-making, but his mood decided how much he gave. Harshada The best presenter, no one could catch her there. But not much coding experience outside Android development. Pranav A jack of all trades with AI and a master of none, and good at presentations. Me Terrible at presentations (though sometimes lucky) and terrible at frontend, but solid at backend and system design. THE CRACKSThe cracks before we even began 💔 Every team has internal conflicts. They don’t matter much when everyone is pulling in the same direction. In our case, a lot was going on underneath, in our friendships and personal lives, and it made it harder and harder to stay together as a team. Vinay and Sharayu couldn’t work with each other, or even talk to each other, because of something between them from the past. Mahesh and I had a problem too. I was deeply hurt because Mahesh had said a few things about me and my career choices to his family, and also told them about our startup. His family then advised him to be less close to Yash and Vinay, and closer to Sharayu, because “that’s where your benefit is.” That sentence stayed in my mind, and it’s still there. But I made one decision: no one would bring their personal conflicts into SIH. I didn’t want old fights ruining this. That’s also why I didn’t push Mahesh too hard on tasks. I was protecting the hackathon, and, if I’m honest, protecting my own hurt feelings too. THE PROBLEMGetting everyone to understand the problem 🗣️ The first big challenge was simply getting everyone to understand the problem statement and what they needed to do. I’ve always been terrible at distributing work. This time I tried hard not to do everything myself, and to let others struggle a little before I jumped in and got my own hands dirty. But first, everyone had to understand the PS. And that took a few days just to arrange, because we couldn’t get everyone into one meeting. Everyone was busy with their own lives. Harshada couldn’t stay after lectures because she lives far away. Pranav couldn’t join online meetings because his house has no network range. And the others, to be honest, didn’t take online meetings seriously. So I decided to explain it all in person. One day, Harshada stayed back after classes, and I explained the problem statement to everyone. And true to my habit of explaining everything, I spoon-fed them the whole soup: what the problem was, what it needed, what we had to do. It was complex for them, and even I was a little confused while explaining. But we got through it somehow. THE REASONSSix people, six reasons 🧭 In the beginning, Mahesh and Pranav showed almost no interest. I’d assign a task and they’d take it lightly, coming back with a one-or-two-prompt ChatGPT answer and saying, “I’ve done the research.” Harshada was the opposite. She kept saying, “Give me a task, give me a task.” But once she had one, she often couldn’t figure out how to do it, and Vinay ended up taking care of it. Sharayu was interactive and built the frontend, but she got very irritated whenever I asked for changes or improvements. Vinay was the only one who did everything I asked, sometimes by his own will, sometimes with a little blackmail 😅, but it was always worth the time. The Mahesh episode. For a while, Mahesh didn’t finish his assigned work, and didn’t even send updates after being reminded several times. So I stopped giving him tasks. He noticed that everyone else had work except him, and he reached out and started asking me to assign him something. I was angry, so I stayed silent. After a while, I sat him down and explained what had gone wrong: he had given no updates at all. His response was that the others weren’t doing anything meaningful either. I told him something I truly believe: I always praise people for trying, not for succeeding. — what I told Mahesh I knew that Harshada had also struggled with her research task, which is why Vinay later took it over. The same with Sharayu: what she tried during research was dismissed later because it wasn’t good enough. But that doesn’t mean they didn’t try. They tried, and they failed. And I appreciate that far more than not trying at all, which is what you did. Mahesh agreed, and from then on he started working normally. The Pranav episode. Pranav did his tasks, but only for the sake of doing them, with no responsibility coming from the heart. He’d paste my questions into ChatGPT or Gemini and send me the output. I told him many times that this wasn’t how it should be done. I asked him to do deep research and then explain me the summary. Instead, he’d read the AI’s whole answer aloud, which I could have done faster and better myself. I was frustrated. When I asked him to give SIH more time, he said he couldn’t, because he had his Civil exam to study for. I asked him to put it aside for just a few days until SIH was over. He didn’t agree. So I stopped forcing him. I was disappointed. I had assumed everyone would give SIH the same dedication and devotion I did. I was wrong. Slowly, I understood what was driving each of them: Pranav wanted to take part in a hackathon, but not to give it his full effort. Sharayu was doing it to feel that she belonged in the group. Harshada was doing it because she had something to prove to Deep. Vinay and Mahesh were doing it because of me. Not one of them had an inner motivation pulling them towards the group’s outcome as a whole. THE PLANThe plan for the internal round 📋 For the internal round, we decided that Harshada, Pranav, Sharayu and I would present. Vinay’s job was to keep Mahesh’s mouth shut. And Mahesh’s job was to stay silent 😅 That sounds like a joke, but it came from experience. Mahesh doesn’t listen to anyone when he wants to prove a point. In our previous SIH, he had actually argued with a judge and told him the judge was wrong. We couldn’t risk that again. We also divided the slides: Harshada: the introduction and a brief explanation of the solution. Me: the overall system and the technical architecture and approach. Sharayu: feasibility and viability. Pranav: the benefits. THE DAYPresentation day 🎤 On the day, I was very tense. I couldn’t remember a single thing I was supposed to say. But we had some luck. Vinay was the SIH coordinator of our class and was already well known among the teachers. Each hall handled 10 to 20 presentations, with one or two judges and faculty members supervising. Vinay was invited to coordinate in one hall, and he asked the teacher to assign him the hall where we’d be presenting, so he could share some insider information and help if needed. Only team leads were allowed to stay during other teams’ presentations, so I stayed and watched the three or four teams that went before us. They were all second-year students, and nobody performed well. That relaxed me a little. Then it was our turn. Harshada delivered her part beautifully. Then I explained the architecture, making eye contact with the judge throughout. At one point I said, “We had a problem here in the flow, and this is how we solved it.” And in that moment, something happened that I’ll never forget. The judge’s face turned curious as I described the problem, and when I mentioned the solution, he smiled back. No words were exchanged, only eyes. It felt like two mature software engineers who had found a flaw in a system design and fixed it together. Sketch of two people facing each other, one explaining and one judging, with a dotted line between their eyes and both smiling problem… solution. no words, just eyes me the judge Fig. 3 — the smile that said more than the slides. Sharayu went next. I had expected better. She sounded like she’d crammed everything and was reciting it. Pranav was a bit nervous, but handled it well. We then moved the judge’s attention from the slides to the printed source documents we’d brought, the charts and sources. He didn’t read through them much, but he still noticed that our data was highly skewed and pointed it out: most of the positive data points lay in one region, while the other regions had almost none. Then came the questions. Harshada made one mistake: she said she had worked on the ML side. We knew she hadn’t been involved in how we researched it. The judge’s natural next question was: “Which other models did you consider for comparison, and what made this one better?” She couldn’t answer. Sharayu tried to help, but we had no idea about ensemble learning, a technique where several models work together, and the model we were using was part of one. So we couldn’t explain it. Still, compared to the presentations before ours, ours was far better. We walked out smiling. Harshada felt guilty about her mistake, and I told her, “Chill. Don’t worry about it.” THE PRAISE“Everyone praised me” 🥹 After the round, everyone in the team praised me for handling the team well. I felt really good, even a little emotional, but I didn’t show it. I just kept a silent smile. I also knew this internal round was nothing compared to what was coming. The real challenge was the PPT screening on the official portal. THE SCORESThe scores that shook us 📉 Some time after our presentation, Vinay called me. He said that a few presentations after ours, including the one by Deep’s group and one other, were really good, and had more marks than us. I was a little sad, but I still believed we’d get through. Harshada heard it differently. She was told that Deep’s group and ours had scored the same marks, which wasn’t actually true. This made her blame herself even more for her mistake in the Q&A. To understand why this hurt her so much, you need to know the story behind it. Harshada and Deep were diploma friends, and both joined our college for degree. In my second-year SIH team, we were all together. This time, they split because of some internal conflicts. Deep said he wouldn’t participate in SIH, so Harshada joined us. A few days later, Deep changed his mind and asked her to come back. She said she couldn’t, because she had already given us her word. There was more to it. In diploma, Harshada, Deep and Shubham (her boyfriend and their diploma classmate) had formed a team and a project together, with a name that carried a lot of memories. They had won a few times at project exhibitions. After Shubham took admission in a different college, the three of them split up, and they agreed that nobody would use that team name or project ahead. But Deep’s SIH team name was the same. It hurt Harshada deeply, but she couldn’t bring herself to say it to him. Later, right after their presentation, Deep’s team came to us full of energy and gave everyone dhokla, saying, “We just cracked it.” It felt like showing off. Deep had also said, indirectly and more than once, that Harshada was only good at presentations, and that winning takes more than that. That’s what Harshada was carrying. She wanted to prove that she could win on her own. THE MARKSThe marks 🤫 That same day, after all the presentations were over, Vinay went to our teacher and requested her to take the marksheet from the external judge, so we could see our marks. After a few requests, she agreed and took the marksheet in her hands. Vinay saw that we had 82 marks, while Deep’s group and one other had 96. He asked the teacher to increase ours a little. He explained that we’d put in a lot of effort that the judge seemed to have missed, and that the judge had under-evaluated us, partly because the few presentations before ours weren’t very impressive. After some back and forth, she agreed. But she said, “Don’t tell anyone about this” 🤐, and took out a bottle of whitener, and changed 82 to 84. That’s how we were shortlisted. Without those two marks, we might have landed on the waiting list. Vinay was then handed the marksheets to deliver to Manish Sir’s cabin (Manish Sir is our SIH coordinator). But Sir was having lunch with all the external judges in the canteen, so Vinay and I went there. Latika Mam, who was having lunch with other faculty members, offered us plates and invited us to join. We politely said no. Out of respect for Manish Sir and the judges, it didn’t feel right to sit and eat with them. THE REBUILDRebuilding the presentation 🛠️ Even before the selection results were out, we’d started preparing for the next stage, the PPT screening. We showed our presentation to my friend Pratik (the former SIH winner), to Manish Sir, and to a few others, and asked for honest reviews. Then we rebuilt the whole presentation around their feedback. We spent almost a full day on a single slide, and then did the same for every other slide. THE MISTAKEThe mistake that was mine 😞 When the results came out, we had to fill in our team details on the official SIH portal. And I made a critical mistake.
